text: The amirs and beys gather in the great tent and raise their new ruler on a white felt, as the steppe has done since the days of Chinggis Khan.
The realm is yours to rule.
Outlast every rival, and Turan will be yours.
The old ruler is gone.
In the great hall the amirs kneel one by one and swear loyalty to the new sovereign.
A new reign begins.
The court weeps around the bier.
The drums are silent, the amirs tear their robes, and the whole realm mourns.
Tomorrow a new ruler will be raised.
Kettle-drums thunder and the long karnay trumpets sound.
The bride arrives under a canopy of silk, and two houses become one family.
A child is born to the royal house.
Midwives sing over the cradle, and the whole court comes to see the baby.
Your banners fly over the citadel.
The city’s elders bring you its keys on a silver dish.
An enemy capital has fallen.
Your banners fly over its citadel, and its people kneel before your governor.
Your army rings the walls.
Engineers raise the catapults, and the defenders shout down from the battlements.
Starve them out, or storm the walls when you are ready.
The envoys exchange sealed letters and robes of honour.
The war is over, and the caravans can travel again.
Carpets are spread in the gardens.
Musicians play, cooks carry out cauldrons of pilaf, and the whole city eats at the ruler’s expense.
For a while, no one has a bad word to say about you.
In the year 1370, the great Chagatai Ulus, heir of Chinggis Khan, lies broken.
Seven crowns rise from its ruins.
The amirs of Samarkand.
The khans of Moghulistan.
The White Horde and the Golden Horde.
The Sufis of Khwarezm, the Kartids of Herat, and the Sarbadars of Sabzevar.
Along the Silk Road, cities change hands with every season.
The caravans pass through towns that may burn tomorrow.
In Samarkand, a lame amir of the Barlas tribe has just been raised on the white felt.
His name is Temur.
Some will win with the sword.
Some with gold and marriages.
Some with poets, astronomers and domes of turquoise.
Only one crown will endure.
Which will be yours?
Rasti rusti.
Strength lies in justice.
If you doubt our power, look at our buildings.
Let the drums sound.
This city is under my protection now.
Let no soldier harm its people.
They chose the sword over mercy.
Let them have the sword.
Tell them: open the gates, and live.
Close them, and the walls will not save you.
We have made peace.
Keep your word, and you will find me a friend.
I swear before God and the amirs: I will hold this land with the sword and with justice.
The city is ours.
Raise our banner over the citadel.
Let the soldiers take their reward.
No wall stands forever.
We will wait, or we will climb.
Let there be peace between us, and let the caravans travel again.
May our two houses be one, and may our sons ride side by side.
Look, my lord: a child for your house.
Your soldiers pour through the broken gates and sack the city.
The loot is carried out by the cartload.
A storyteller will read the great scenes and the turning points of history aloud.
One of the most learned men of his age, master of logic, rhetoric and law, honoured at Temur's court in Samarkand.
A great master of logic, grammar and theology.
Temur brought him from Shiraz to teach in Samarkand.
A mathematician and astronomer from Bursa who came to Samarkand.
He later taught Ulugh Beg and helped found his observatory.
A brilliant mathematician and astronomer who calculated the number π to sixteen places, a record that stood for two centuries.
The greatest lyric poet of Persia.
A famous legend tells how he met Temur in Shiraz.
A poet born in Khujand who lived in Tabriz, admired for his short, polished ghazals.
The finest musician and composer of his time, who wrote books on the theory of music and played at the courts of Tabriz and Samarkand.
A master painter of Baghdad and Tabriz whom Temur brought to Samarkand.
His pupils founded the great school of Persian miniature painting.
A poet of Herat who wrote in Chagatai Turki.
Alisher Navoi later called him the king of the poets of his age.
A historian whom Temur commissioned to write the Zafarnama, the Book of Victories, in plain Persian.
A historian and poet who wrote the most famous Zafarnama, the Book of Victories, the great history of Temur's life.
The North African historian and thinker.
In 1401, outside Damascus, he spent weeks in conversation with Temur.
Envoy of King Henry III of Castile.
His account of Temur's court in Samarkand in 1404 is one of the best we have.
Instruments, books and pupils follow him.
Your court is becoming a place of learning.
Ruins of Afrasiyab
On the hill of Afrasiyab, where old Samarkand stood before the Mongols came, diggers break into a sealed hall.
Its walls are painted with Sogdian kings riding elephants, and in a corner stands a jar full of ancient silver.
Mausoleum of the Samanids
The tomb of Ismail Samani, built of baked brick woven like a basket, has stood in Bukhara for four hundred years.
Its keepers ask for help: the dome is cracked and pilgrims fear it will fall.
The Iron Gate
The Iron Gate is a gorge so narrow that two camels can barely pass.
Whoever holds it holds the road from Samarkand to India.
Your officers propose to close it with real gates of iron.
Pastures of the Heavenly Horses
In the meadows of Fergana graze the famous "heavenly horses" that sweat blood when they run.
Chinese emperors once sent armies across the mountains to get them.
The herdsmen bring you the finest herd of the year.
The Sunken City of Issyk-Kul
Fishermen on the Issyk-Kul, the lake that never freezes, pull up bronze cauldrons and old bricks in their nets.
They say a whole city lies under the water, drowned for the sins of its king.
Tash Rabat
At Tash Rabat, a stone caravanserai high in the mountains on the road to China, a snowstorm has trapped a great caravan.
Its merchants send a rider down to beg for help.
Jade Rivers of Khotan
The spring floods have brought down from the Kunlun mountains a block of dark green jade as big as a man.
Chinese merchants are already offering a fortune for it.
Ulytau, Mountain of the Khans
At Ulytau, among the sacred mountains, stands the tomb of Jochi, eldest son of Chinggis Khan.
The elders of the steppe say a ruler who is raised on a white felt here rules with heaven’s blessing.
Sturgeon Fisheries of the Volga
Fishermen of the Volga delta have caught a beluga sturgeon longer than three men.
Its roe alone fills twenty barrels.
Fortresses of Ayaz-Kala
On the edge of the Kyzylkum stand the ruined fortresses of Ayaz-Kala, built by the old kings of Khwarezm a thousand years ago.
Their walls of mud brick still rise over the sands.
The Giants of Bamiyan
In the valley of Bamiyan two giant figures, taller than any minaret, stand carved into the red cliff.
Around them are hundreds of caves painted by monks who left long ago.
Your amirs ask what should be done with them.
Turquoise Mines of Nishapur
The miners of Nishapur have found a vein of turquoise of the purest sky blue.
Such stones are worth more than gold in Tabriz and Cairo.
Lapis Mines of Sar-i Sang
High in the mountains of Badakhshan, at Sar-i Sang, miners break the deep-blue lapis lazuli out of the rock with fire and cold water.
Painters from Herat to Venice cannot work without it.
Ruins of Old Merv
Old Merv was once among the greatest cities in the world, until the Mongols destroyed it in 1221.
Now the dome of Sultan Sanjar’s tomb rises over empty walls, and the great dam on the Murghab lies broken.
Golden Kurgans of the Altai
In the valley of the Irtysh stand great burial mounds of steppe kings who lived long before Chinggis Khan.
The herdsmen say they are full of gold, and that the dead do not like to be disturbed.
The old coins pour into your treasury.
The painted kings watch in silence.
Scholars copy the paintings.
Poets compare your reign to the kings of old.
Masons from Bukhara mend the dome brick by brick.
Pilgrims pray for you at the tomb.
The keepers bow and say nothing.
Iron-bound gates now close the gorge.
No army will pass without your leave.
The toll from the Iron Gate is paid.
Your toll collectors take their places in the gorge.
Your new riders gallop across the meadows, their horses gleaming with sweat.
There is no one worthy of such a gift.
The divers come up with golden bowls and the seal of a forgotten king.
The water is cold and dark.
The divers find only stones.
The fishermen say the lake will be kind to you.
The merchants rescued at Tash Rabat repay your kindness.
Your men dig the caravan out of the snow.
The merchants swear they will not forget.
The storm passes.
Not every camel survives it.
The stone leaves for China on a cart drawn by twelve oxen.
Your new jade throne is the wonder of every ambassador who sees it.
The beys lift you on the white felt as the drums thunder.
The steppe has a khan.
You leave a horse and a silk banner at the tomb.
For three days the city eats sturgeon and sings your name.
The Genoese pay in Venetian ducats and ask for more.
Watchmen climb the old towers again.
Their fires can be seen across the desert.
Beneath a fallen tower your men find a hoard of silver dirhams.
Only sand, scorpions and broken pots.
Your decree is carved at the foot of the cliff: let no one harm the giants of Bamiyan.
Soldiers move into the painted caves.
Bamiyan becomes a fortress.
Merchants from Tabriz buy the whole vein before it is even dug out.
A dome of turquoise rises over Nishapur, the colour of heaven itself.
Your painters grind the stone into the finest ultramarine.
Your palaces glow blue and gold.
The blue stones travel west, worth their weight in gold.
Water flows again through the canals of Merv.
Farmers return to the empty fields.
Caravans of carts carry the old bricks to build a new bazaar.
Golden stags and griffins are carried out of the mounds.
The tribes whisper of a curse.
The shamans bless your name at the kurgans.
All your cities celebrate, and the bride’s family is honoured.
For forty days the city feasts in gardens hung with silk.
Wrestlers, acrobats and poets compete for the newlyweds’ favour.
Nothing changes.
The vows are spoken before the qadi, and the couple begin their life together.
The fugitive prince
Toqtamish, a young prince of the line of Chinggis Khan, has fled to your court after Urus Khan beat him.
He begs for men and horses to win back his inheritance.
History remembers what Temur chose, and that the prince he raised up later turned against him.
Amir Temur gives the fugitive prince Toqtamish an army to win back the White Horde.
Amir Temur hands the fugitive prince Toqtamish over to Urus Khan.
Amir Temur keeps the fugitive prince Toqtamish at his court as a general.
Your rival Toqtamish has escaped to the court of Amir Temur, who is giving him men and horses.
As long as he lives, there is a claimant to your throne.
Kath and Khiva
Husayn Sufi of Khwarezm will not give back Kath and Khiva.
Your amirs want war.
Your wise men say there is another way: Khanzade, the famous beauty of Urgench, is of age, and your son Jahangir has no wife.
Amir Temur marches on Khwarezm to take back Kath and Khiva.
Amir Temur asks for Khanzade of Khwarezm as a bride for his son Jahangir.
Peace is made.
Amir Temur buys Kath back from Khwarezm with gold.
Temur’s envoy
Temur’s envoy stands in your hall in Urgench and demands Kath and Khiva back.
In history, Husayn Sufi called him a rebel who rose by the sword and told him to come and fight.
Moscow refuses tribute
Prince Dmitry of Moscow will no longer pay the tribute the Horde has taken for a hundred and forty years.
The amirs call for a great campaign to burn Moscow.
In history it ended on the field of Kulikovo.
Mamai leads the Golden Horde against Moscow.
Mamai marches on Moscow with Lithuania as his ally.
Mamai forgives Moscow its tribute.
There will be no great battle this year.
A summons from Temur
Temur summons you to his kurultai, to bow as his vassal.
In history, the malik of Herat delayed and strengthened his walls, and Herat fell in 1381.
The malik of Herat refuses to bow to Temur and strengthens his walls.
The malik of Herat bows to Temur and becomes his ally.
The Kartids and the Sarbadars ally against Temur.
Temur in Khorasan
Temur’s army is in Khorasan.
In history, Khwaja Ali Mu’ayyad rode out to meet him and submitted, and kept his city.
Khwaja Ali Mu’ayyad of the Sarbadars submits to Temur.
The Sarbadars refuse to submit to Temur and prepare for a siege.
The Sarbadars call their dervishes to holy war against Temur.
Temur asks for a bride
Temur’s envoys ask for the hand of your daughter Tukal Khanum.
In history she married him in 1397, and the long wars between Moghulistan and Samarkand came to an end.
Khizr Khoja of Moghulistan sends his daughter Tukal Khanum to marry Temur.
The old enemies make peace.
Moghulistan refuses Temur’s offer of marriage and raids Transoxiana.
Khizr Khoja turns away from Temur and wages holy war on the Uyghur cities.
The march on China
The Ming emperor demands that you pay him tribute.
You are nearly seventy.
Your amirs have gathered two hundred thousand men for a winter march on China.
In history, Temur fell ill at Otrar and died in February 1405.
Amir Temur marches on China in the depth of winter.
Amir Temur puts off his campaign against China until spring.
Amir Temur gives up the march on China and settles his succession.
Cracks in the dome
Cracks run through the great dome of the Bibi-Khanym mosque.
It was raised too fast, and bricks fall on the worshippers.
In history, Temur had the builders punished and the mosque began to crumble within a few years.
History takes another path
Toqtamish rides north with your horsemen.
If he wins, the steppe will owe you a debt.
Toqtamish is sent north in chains.
Urus Khan sends you a herd of white horses in thanks.
Toqtamish swears to serve you.
He takes command of a regiment of steppe horsemen.
Your scouts watch the road from Otrar.
Toqtamish will come.
Temur does not want a war with the steppe.
Toqtamish is sent to you in chains.
Temur laughs at your envoys.
Toqtamish will come, with Temur’s horsemen behind him.
Toqtamish is found dead in his tent near Otrar.
No one saw the killer.
The assassins are caught and confess.
Temur gives Toqtamish even more men.
Your army gathers on the Amu Darya.
The Sufi dynasty will answer for its pride.
The wedding is the most splendid the steppe has seen.
Khwarezm and the Chagatai Ulus are bound by blood.
Husayn Sufi counts the gold and hands over the keys of Kath.
The envoy rides away.
By spring, Temur’s army is on the Amu Darya.
Khanzade rides to Samarkand with a dowry of gold and pearls.
There is peace, for now.
Kath goes to Temur.
He sends a robe of honour in return.
The Horde rides west, with Genoese foot soldiers and Circassian horsemen.
Grand Duke Jogaila promises to bring his army to the Don.
Moscow keeps its silver.
In the Horde, men mutter that the old days are over.
Masons work day and night on the walls of Herat.
You kneel before Temur’s throne.
He raises you up and calls you his son.
Envoys ride to Sabzevar.
Khorasan will stand together.
Temur receives you kindly.
Sabzevar is spared.
“We would rather hang than submit,” the people shout, as their fathers did.
The dervishes leave their lodges with swords in their hands.
Tukal Khanum leaves for Samarkand with a great train of horses.
The steppe is at peace.
Your riders burn the villages of Fergana and come home with loot.
Your army rides east to Turfan and returns with gold and captives.
The snow lies deep at Otrar.
The old conqueror catches a fever and dies.
The great army turns back.
Against all fears you cross the mountains.
The frightened Ming emperor sends silk, silver and porcelain to keep you away.
You spend the winter in your gardens in Samarkand.
The campaign can wait.
The master builders are dragged before you.
New plaster covers the cracks, for now.
The best masons of Tabriz and Delhi raise the dome again, slowly and well.
It will stand.
The imams pray for the dome.
The cracks grow wider.
This is not what happened in our history.
The ungrateful khan
Toqtamish, whom Temur raised to the throne of the steppe, has turned against his patron.
His horsemen cross the Syr Darya to plunder Transoxiana.
Toqtamish attacks
With Temur’s horsemen behind him, Toqtamish crosses into the White Horde to claim the throne.
The dome falls
With a roar heard across Samarkand, the great dome of the Bibi-Khanym mosque collapses.
The wonder is lost.
Urus Khan dies in the winter of 1377.
Without Toqtamish to challenge them, his son Temur-Malik takes the throne of the White Horde.
No battle at Kulikovo
The Horde did not march this year.
Moscow keeps its silver, and its army waits.
Kulikovo: no victor
With the Lithuanians at his side, Mamai fights Prince Dmitry on the Don.
Both armies bleed, and neither can claim the field.
Mamai wins at Kulikovo
Against what history remembers, Mamai’s horsemen break the Russian line on the field of Kulikovo.
Moscow pays double tribute.
Kurultai at Balkh
In April 1370 the amirs of the Chagatai Ulus gather at Balkh and proclaim Temur their Great Amir.
A descendant of Ögedei, Soyurghatmish, is raised as puppet khan.
Khwarezm defies Temur
Husayn Sufi refuses to hand back Kath and Khiva to the Chagatai Ulus.
Temur swears to take them by force.
Urus Khan marches on Sarai
Urus Khan of the White Horde drives Mamai's puppet khan from Sarai and claims the throne of all the Jochids.
Toqtamish flees to Temur
The young Jochid prince Toqtamish, defeated by Urus Khan, takes refuge at Temur's court.
Temur gives him Otrar and Sauran and an army.
Death of Urus Khan
His sons quarrel over the throne, and the White Horde is shaken.
Battle of Kulikovo
On the field of Kulikovo, Prince Dmitry of Moscow defeats Mamai.
The Golden Horde loses many of its best riders.
Plague on the Silk Road
The Black Death returns along the caravan routes.
Towns on the Silk Road lose many of their people.
A great caravan from China
A rich caravan arrives from Ming China, bringing silk and porcelain to the bazaars of the west.
Bibi-Khanym rises in Samarkand
Masons from across the conquered lands raise a great congregational mosque in Samarkand.
Whoever holds the city gains prestige.

Houses of healing
School of engineers
Astronomical tables
The great observatory
Court poets
The royal library
Scribes copy your chronicles for foreign courts: every ruler thinks a little better of you each turn.
School of miniature painting
Golden age of verse
Poets in Persian and Turki compete for your favour: other rulers value any deal with you more.
Capital of the arts
Caravanserais
Silver tanga
Craft guilds
Bills of exchange
Merchants pay with paper instead of silver: a large treasury loses half as much, and only above 9,000 gold.
Crossroads of the world
Courts of the qadis
Post roads
Relay stations carry your orders quickly: the realm can hold 4 more cities before it grows too large.
The divan
A chancellery of trained officials: governors cost half as much and keep 4 more order.
The code of law
One law for amir and peasant: revolts are half as likely.
Imperial administration
Bibi-Khanym Mosque
The vast congregational mosque of Samarkand.
Ak-Saray Palace
The White Palace of Shahrisabz, with its towering portal.
Every general you appoint starts with an extra star.
Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmad Yasawi
The shrine of the great Turkic Sufi poet, near Otrar.
Musalla of Herat
A complex of madrasas and slender minarets.
Grand Bazaar of Sarai
The greatest market of the northern Silk Road.
The Conquest of Khwarezm
Husayn Sufi of Khwarezm refuses to return Kath and Khiva to the Chagatai Ulus.
Temur swears to take the whole oasis of the lower Amu Darya, with its rich capital Urgench.
History gave him eight years.
Toqtamish and the Golden Throne
Urus Khan is dead.
The young Toqtamish, a prince of the house of Jochi who once fled to Temur, now holds the White Horde.
Beyond the Volga, Mamai rules Sarai through puppet khans.
Your riders have already crossed the Yaik and taken Saraichik.
Unite the two halves of the Horde of Jochi.
The Khan Strikes Back
Twice the Moghul khans conquered Transoxiana, and twice the amirs of Samarkand drove them out.
Now Qamar al-Din Dughlat rules the steppe, and the upstart Temur sits in Samarkand.
Take back the cities of the Chagatai Ulus.
The Last Sarbadars
The Sarbadars of Sabzevar, a republic of rebels who chose death over Mongol tribute, have ruled western Khorasan for forty years.
Now the Kartids of Herat press from the east, and a far greater storm is rising beyond the Amu Darya.
Herat, City of Poets
Herat is small in land but great in learning: its madrasas, painters and poets are famous from Tabriz to Delhi.
Malik Ghiyath al-Din can never outfight his neighbours.
He can outshine them.
The Ungrateful Khan
Toqtamish owes his throne to Temur, and he has not forgotten it: he hates him for it.
Now he rules the whole Horde of Jochi, from the Volga to the Syr Darya.
Temur and his best men are far away in Persia.
This winter the Horde rides south.
Bukhara, Tashkent and Otrar fly the banners of the Horde.
In history Toqtamish burned the palaces of Transoxiana and then fled before Temur’s return.
In this story, the Chagatai Ulus has lost its heart, and the steppe rules the cities once more.
The Sack of Sarai
On the Terek, in April 1395, Temur has broken the army of Toqtamish.
The khan has fled into the steppe.
Now the road lies open to Sarai, the richest city of the north, where the Horde keeps the treasure of a hundred and fifty years.
Sarai burns, and Hajji-Tarkhan with it.
The Golden Horde never recovers: its trade turns away to new roads, and the steppe empire of Batu fades.
Temur rides home to Samarkand with the craftsmen of the north in his train.
The Heirs of Temur
In February 1405 Temur died at Otrar, on his way to China.
His grandson Khalil Sultan has seized Samarkand and the treasury, and scatters gold to win the amirs.
In Herat, Temur’s youngest son, Shah Rukh, gathers the army of Khorasan.
Shah Rukh enters Samarkand in 1409 and gives it to his son Ulugh Beg.
He rules the empire of Temur from Herat for forty years, in peace, among poets, painters and builders.
The age of the sword gives way to the age of the book.
Ulugh Beg’s Samarkand
Samarkand has a new master: Ulugh Beg, grandson of Temur, fifteen years old, who loves the stars more than the sword.
Around him gather mathematicians and astronomers.
Make his city the capital of learning of the whole world.
On a hill above Samarkand rises the great observatory, with a sextant forty metres high.
Ulugh Beg’s star tables, the most exact since Ptolemy, are copied in Istanbul, in Delhi and, centuries later, in Oxford.
Temur returns
Riders bring the news: Temur has crossed the Amu Darya with the army of Persia, and he is marching north.

Davlat sizning qo‘lingizda.

Eski hukmdor bu dunyodan o‘tdi.

Saroy tobut atrofida yig‘lamoqda.
Nog‘oralar jim, amirlar to‘nlarini yirtmoqda, butun mamlakat motam tutmoqda.

Dushman poytaxti quladi.

Qo‘shiningiz devorlarni o‘rab oldi.
Muhandislar manjaniqlarni o‘rnatmoqda, himoyachilar esa qal’a devorlaridan baqirmoqda.
Ularni ochlik bilan bo‘ysundiring yoki tayyor bo‘lganingizda devorlarga hujum qiling.
Elchilar muhrlangan maktublar va xil’atlar almashadi.
Urush tugadi, karvonlar yana yo‘lga chiqishi mumkin.
Bog‘larda gilamlar to‘shalgan.
Sozandalar chalmoqda, oshpazlar qozon-qozon palov olib chiqmoqda, butun shahar hukmdor hisobidan to‘yib yemoqda.
Bir muddat hech kim siz haqingizda yomon so‘z aytmaydi.
Chingizxon merosi bo‘lgan buyuk Chig‘atoy ulusi parchalanib yotibdi.
Uning xarobalaridan yetti toj ko‘tariladi.
Samarqand amirlari.
Mo‘g‘uliston xonlari.
Oq O‘rda va Oltin O‘rda.
Xorazm So‘fiylari, Hirot Kartlari va Sabzavor sarbadorlari.
Ipak yo‘li bo‘ylab shaharlar har faslda qo‘ldan-qo‘lga o‘tadi.
Karvonlar ertaga yonib ketishi mumkin bo‘lgan shaharlardan o‘tib boradi.
Samarqandda barlos qabilasidan bo‘lgan oqsoq amir hozirgina oq kigizda ko‘tarildi.
Uning ismi Temur.
Kimdir qilich bilan g‘alaba qozonadi.
Kimdir oltin va nikohlar bilan.
Kimdir esa shoirlar, munajjimlar va feruza gumbazlar bilan.
Faqat bitta toj qoladi.
Qaysi biri sizniki bo‘ladi?
Rosti-rusti.
Kuch adolatdadir.
Agar qudratimizga shubhang bo‘lsa, binolarimizga boq.
Nog‘oralar chalinsin.
Bu shahar endi mening himoyamda.
Hech bir askar uning xalqiga zarar yetkazmasin.
Ular shafqatdan ko‘ra qilichni tanladilar.
Qilich ularniki bo‘lsin.
Ularga ayting: darvozani ochsalar, omon qoladilar.
Yopsalar, devorlar ularni qutqarmaydi.
Sulh tuzdik.
So‘zingda tursang, meni do‘st deb bilasan.
Olloh va amirlar oldida qasam ichaman: bu yurtni qilich va adolat bilan saqlayman.
Shahar bizniki.
Bayrog‘imizni qal’a ustiga tiking.
Askarlar o‘z mukofotini olsin.
Hech bir devor abadiy turmaydi.
Kutamiz yoki oshib o‘tamiz.
Oramizda tinchlik bo‘lsin, karvonlar yana yo‘lga chiqsin.

Moğol haracı yerine ölümü seçen asilerin cumhuriyeti olan Sebzevar Serbedarları kırk yıldır batı Horasan’ı yönetiyor.
Şimdi doğudan Herat Kartları sıkıştırıyor, Amuderya’nın ötesinde ise çok daha büyük bir fırtına yükseliyor.
Şairler şehri Herat
Herat’ın toprağı küçük ama ilmi büyük: medreseleri, ressamları ve şairleri Tebriz’den Delhi’ye kadar ünlü.
Melik Gıyaseddin komşularını savaşta asla yenemez.
Ama onları parlaklıkta geçebilir.
Nankör Han
Toktamış tahtını Timur'a borçlu ve bunu unutmadı: tam da bu yüzden ondan nefret ediyor.
Artık İdil'den Seyhun'a kadar bütün Cuci Ordası'na hükmediyor.
Timur ve en iyi adamları uzakta, İran'da.
Bu kış Orda güneye akıyor.
Buhara, Taşkent ve Otrar'da Orda'nın sancakları dalgalanıyor.
Tarihte Toktamış Maveraünnehir'in saraylarını yakmış, Timur dönmeden kaçmıştı.
Bu hikâyede ise Çağatay Ulusu kalbini yitirdi ve bozkır şehirlere yeniden hükmediyor.
Saray'ın Yağması
Nisan 1395'te Terek kıyısında Timur, Toktamış'ın ordusunu ezdi.
Han bozkıra kaçtı.
Şimdi kuzeyin en zengin şehri Saray'a, Orda'nın yüz elli yıllık hazinesini sakladığı yere giden yol açık.
Saray yanıyor, onunla birlikte Hacı Tarhan da.
Altın Orda bir daha toparlanamaz: ticareti yeni yollara döner ve Batu'nun bozkır imparatorluğu söner.
Timur kuzeyin zanaatkârlarını peşine takarak Semerkant'a döner.
Timur'un Varisleri
Şubat 1405'te Timur, Çin seferi yolunda Otrar'da öldü.
Torunu Halil Sultan Semerkant'ı ve hazineyi ele geçirdi, emirleri kazanmak için altın saçıyor.
Herat'ta ise Timur'un en küçük oğlu Şahruh, Horasan ordusunu topluyor.
Şahruh 1409'da Semerkant'a girer ve şehri oğlu Uluğ Bey'e verir.
Timur'un imparatorluğunu kırk yıl boyunca Herat'tan, barış içinde, şairler, ressamlar ve mimarlar arasında yönetir.
Kılıç çağı yerini kitap çağına bırakır.
Uluğ Bey'in Semerkant'ı
Semerkant'ın yeni efendisi Timur'un on beş yaşındaki torunu Uluğ Bey; yıldızları kılıçtan çok seviyor.
Çevresinde matematikçiler ve gökbilimciler toplanıyor.
Onun şehrini bütün dünyanın ilim başkenti yap.
Semerkant'ın üstündeki tepede kırk metre yüksekliğinde sekstantıyla büyük rasathane yükseliyor.
Batlamyus'tan beri en doğru olan Uluğ Bey'in yıldız cetvelleri İstanbul'da, Delhi'de ve yüzyıllar sonra Oxford'da kopyalanıyor.
Timur dönüyor
Ulaklar haber getirir: Timur İran ordusuyla Ceyhun'u geçti ve kuzeye yürüyor.
